items.followUp: Name and briefly describe five branches of biology.

rubric.why: Credits correctly named and described branches concerned with form and structure.
rubric.description: Describes two branches from morphology, anatomy, and histology.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for two correctly named branches with their corresponding meanings.

rubric.why: Credits correctly named and described branches concerned with cells, functions, or inheritance.
rubric.description: Describes two branches from cytology, physiology, and genetics.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for two correctly named branches with their corresponding meanings.

rubric.why: Credits correctly named and described branches concerned with classification, environment, or fossils.
rubric.description: Describes two branches from taxonomy, ecology, and palaeontology.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for two correctly named branches with their corresponding meanings.

rubric.why: Credits correctly named and described further branches of biology.
rubric.description: Describes two further branches of biology.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for two correctly named branches with their corresponding meanings.

modelAnswer: Morphology is the study of the form and external structure of organisms.
Anatomy is the study of the internal structure of organisms.
Histology is the study of tissues.
Cytology is the study of cells.
Physiology is the study of the functions of living organisms and their parts.
Genetics is the study of heredity and variation.
Taxonomy is the identification, naming, and classification of organisms.
Embryology is the study of the development of an embryo.
Ecology is the study of the relationships of organisms with one another and their environment.
Palaeontology is the study of fossils.
Microbiology is the study of microorganisms.
Parasitology is the study of parasites and their relationships with hosts.
Biotechnology is the use of organisms or biological processes for human benefit.

items.followUp: State two functions of mitochondria and name two parts visible in a mitochondrion diagram.

rubric.why: Identifies mitochondria as organelles involved in aerobic respiration and energy production.
rubric.description: Defines mitochondria as organelles involved in aerobic respiration or ATP production.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a suitable definition identifying aerobic respiration or ATP production.

rubric.why: Recognises the two membranes enclosing the mitochondrion.
rubric.description: Identifies the outer and inner membranes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying both membranes.

rubric.why: Recognises characteristic internal parts of a mitochondrion.
rubric.description: Identifies cristae and an internal region or space in the diagram or description.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly identifying the cristae and the matrix or intermembrane space.

rubric.why: Explains a structural feature or identifies the matrix contents.
rubric.description: Explains that cristae provide a large surface area or that the matrix contains respiratory enzymes.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for either valid structural detail.

rubric.why: States the useful energy-carrying product of mitochondrial respiration.
rubric.description: States that mitochondria produce ATP to supply energy for cellular activities.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying ATP as the energy-carrying product.

modelAnswer: Mitochondria are double-membrane-bound organelles in eukaryotic cells where aerobic respiration releases energy and ATP is produced.
The outer membrane encloses the organelle; the folded inner membrane forms cristae, and the inner fluid-filled region is the matrix.

Diagram (labelled schematic): draw an oval mitochondrion; draw a smooth outer boundary labelled outer membrane; draw a second inner boundary folded inward and label the folds cristae; label the gap between the two membranes intermembrane space; label the interior matrix.
The cristae provide a large surface area for reactions of cellular respiration, while the matrix contains enzymes involved in respiration.
Mitochondria are therefore called the powerhouses of the cell because they supply ATP for cellular activities.

items.followUp: Write the rules for formatting the scientific name of an organism and give one example.

rubric.why: Defines the two-part scientific naming system and identifies its components.
rubric.description: Defines binomial nomenclature as a system in which each organism has a two-word scientific name: genus and species.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for the two-word definition with both components; award 1 mark if the two-part nature is stated but a component is missing.

rubric.why: Explains why scientific names are useful across languages and regions.
rubric.description: States that scientific names are internationally accepted and avoid confusion caused by local or common names.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid significance.

rubric.why: Shows correct conventions for writing a scientific name.
rubric.description: States the capitalization convention and that scientific names are italicised in print or underlined when handwritten.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the capitalization and italicising or underlining conventions.

modelAnswer: Binomial nomenclature is the system of naming each organism with a scientific name consisting of two words.
The first word is the genus name and the second word is the species name; for example, *Homo sapiens*.
The genus begins with a capital letter and the species name with a lower-case letter. The two words are italicised in print or underlined separately when handwritten.
It provides organisms with internationally accepted names and avoids confusion caused by different local or common names.

items.followUp: Explain how carbon dioxide is converted into carbohydrate during the Calvin cycle.

rubric.why: Identifies the location and light-independent nature of the dark reaction.
rubric.description: States that the dark reaction takes place in the chloroplast stroma and does not directly require light.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying both its location and light-independent nature.

rubric.why: Describes carbon fixation, the first stage of the cycle.
rubric.description: States that carbon dioxide is fixed with RuBP, a five-carbon compound, to form an unstable six-carbon compound.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly describing carbon dioxide fixation with RuBP or the five-carbon acceptor.

rubric.why: Identifies the energy and reducing power used by the cycle.
rubric.description: States that ATP and NADPH from the light reaction are used in the dark reaction.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for naming both ATP and NADPH as inputs.

rubric.why: Identifies the carbohydrate product formed from fixed carbon.
rubric.description: States that G3P is used to form carbohydrates or sugar.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying G3P or sugar as a carbohydrate product or precursor.

rubric.why: Recognises regeneration of the carbon dioxide acceptor so the cycle can continue.
rubric.description: States that RuBP is regenerated.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying regeneration of RuBP.

modelAnswer: The dark reaction, or Calvin cycle, occurs in the stroma of chloroplasts and does not directly require light.
Carbon dioxide is fixed when it combines with RuBP, a five-carbon compound, to form an unstable six-carbon compound that splits into two molecules of 3-PGA.
ATP and NADPH made during the light reaction provide energy and reducing power to convert 3-PGA into G3P.
Some G3P is used to form carbohydrates, while the remaining G3P is used with ATP to regenerate RuBP.
The regenerated RuBP combines with more carbon dioxide, allowing the cycle to continue.

items.followUp: Explain one benefit of fertilizers and two environmental problems caused by their excessive use.

rubric.why: Defines fertilizers by their role in supplying nutrients.
rubric.description: Defines fertilizers as materials added to soil or plants to supply mineral nutrients and support growth.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for defining fertilizers as nutrient-supplying materials.

rubric.why: States their agricultural importance.
rubric.description: Explains that fertilizers promote plant growth and improve crop yield.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a valid benefit.

rubric.why: Identifies nutrient pollution of water as an environmental hazard.
rubric.description: Explains that fertilizer runoff or excess nutrients can cause algal blooms or eutrophication.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking excess nutrients or runoff to eutrophication or algal blooms.

rubric.why: Identifies a further environmental hazard of excessive fertilizer use.
rubric.description: States that fertilizers can contaminate groundwater or drinking water, or damage or acidify soil.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one valid additional hazard.

modelAnswer: Fertilizers are natural or synthetic substances added to soil or plants to supply essential mineral nutrients.
They promote plant growth and increase the yield of crops.
Excess fertilizer may be washed into rivers and lakes; excess nutrients can cause algal blooms and eutrophication, reducing oxygen in the water and harming aquatic life.
Nitrates may also leach into groundwater and contaminate drinking water; excessive use can also damage or acidify soil.

items.followUp: Which antigens and antibodies are present in blood groups A and B, and why must donor blood be checked before transfusion?

rubric.why: Identifies the basis of ABO classification.
rubric.description: Explains that ABO groups are determined by antigens on red blood cells and antibodies in plasma.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly distinguishing red-cell antigens from plasma antibodies.

rubric.why: Gives the antigen-antibody pattern for groups A and B.
rubric.description: States that group A has A antigen and anti-B antibody, while group B has B antigen and anti-A antibody.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for both patterns correctly stated.

rubric.why: Gives the antigen-antibody pattern for groups AB and O.
rubric.description: States that AB has both antigens and neither antibody, while O has neither antigen and both antibodies.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for both patterns correctly stated.

rubric.why: Recognises the basic red-cell transfusion compatibility roles in the ABO system.
rubric.description: Identifies O as the universal red-cell donor and AB as the universal red-cell recipient in the ABO system.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for both compatibility roles.

rubric.why: Explains the danger of incompatible transfusion.
rubric.description: States that incompatible blood can cause an antigen-antibody reaction and agglutination of red blood cells.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for explaining the risk of agglutination or another harmful antigen-antibody reaction.

modelAnswer: The ABO blood group system classifies blood according to antigens on red blood cells and antibodies in the plasma.
Group A: A antigen on red blood cells; anti-B antibody in plasma. Group B: B antigen; anti-A antibody.
Group AB: both A and B antigens; no anti-A or anti-B antibodies. Group O: neither A nor B antigen; both anti-A and anti-B antibodies.
For red-cell transfusions in the ABO system, group O is the universal donor and group AB is the universal recipient; Rh factor must also be considered in practice.
Donor and recipient blood must be compatible because an antigen-antibody reaction can cause red blood cells to agglutinate and may seriously harm the recipient.
